name: Spironolactone
lead: Spironolactone (brand name Aldactone, among others) is a prescription steroidal medication that blocks aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor and, to a lesser degree, blocks androgen receptors [1][2]. Its labelled uses are cardiovascular and renal: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, add-on treatment of hypertension, and oedema in cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome, with other approved uses including primary hyperaldosteronism and low potassium [1][3].

In appearance medicine it is used off-label as an antiandrogen, mainly for persistent acne in adult women, and also for hirsutism and female pattern hair loss [1][4]. The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline makes a conditional recommendation for spironolactone, and two randomised trials, the SAFA trial in England and Wales and the FASCE trial in France, have tested it in adult women with acne [4][5][6].

Prescribing information warns of hyperkalaemia and recommends potassium monitoring, notes that it can cause gynecomastia, and reports feminisation of male fetuses in rat studies [3]. Wikipedia notes it was discovered in 1957 and introduced in 1959 [1].
infobox: Oral (topical forms exist in some places) [1]
Not recommended; theoretical feminisation of a male fetus [1][3]

paras: The US label lists heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (NYHA class III to IV), add-on therapy for hypertension, oedema in cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome, and primary hyperaldosteronism among its indications [3]. The 1999 RALES trial in 1,663 people with severe heart failure was stopped early after a 30 percent relative reduction in death with spironolactone versus placebo [7]. In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, the TOPCAT trial found no significant reduction in its primary composite outcome (18.6 percent versus 20.4 percent) [8]. In resistant hypertension the PATHWAY-2 crossover trial found spironolactone superior to placebo, bisoprolol and doxazosin as add-on therapy [9], and a 2025 JAMA trial compared it with amiloride [10]. Spironolactone is also used in feminising hormone therapy as an antiandrogen [1].

Wikipedia describes androgens as central to oily skin, acne, hirsutism and male pattern hair loss, and notes that spironolactone is used for acne in women and sometimes combined with a contraceptive pill, with benefit potentially taking up to about three months to appear [1]. It is described as a first-line treatment for hirsutism and has been compared with finasteride, flutamide and cyproterone acetate in that setting [1]. A 2023 systematic review examined oral and topical spironolactone for androgenetic alopecia, and a broader 2024 review of hair-loss treatments lists a range of options [11][12]. A 2017 retrospective study described outcomes in 110 women treated for acne [13]. Because of its antiandrogen effects, it is generally not used for acne in men, according to prescribing overviews [1][14].

The SAFA trial was a pragmatic, multicentre, phase 3, double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial of spironolactone in women with acne vulgaris in England and Wales, published in the BMJ in 2023 [5]. The FASCE study, a multicentre randomised double-blind trial, compared spironolactone with doxycycline in moderate acne in adult women and was published in 2024 [6]. A 2012 practical review earlier summarised the observational data for post-teenage women [14].

The 2024 AAD guideline places spironolactone in its conditional recommendations, alongside combined oral contraceptives, sarecycline and minocycline [4]. A 2025 review of acne innovations discusses opportunities to improve patient experience with spironolactone [15], and a 2026 editorial in the same journal discusses the drug's role in acne [16].
For hair loss, evidence comes mainly from small studies summarised in a systematic review of oral and topical use [11]. A registered trial of spironolactone for melasma was withdrawn [17].

The label lists hyperkalaemia, hypotension and worsening renal function, electrolyte and metabolic abnormalities, and gynecomastia as clinically significant adverse reactions, and advises monitoring of potassium within a week of starting and periodically afterwards. Risk of hyperkalaemia rises with renal impairment, potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes [3]. Other reported effects include nausea, headache, rash, reduced libido and, as noted in dermatology overviews, menstrual irregularity and breast tenderness [1][2]. A population study found hospitalisation for hyperkalaemia rose after publication of RALES as prescribing increased [18].

Pregnancy: rat studies report feminisation of male fetuses, and the label advises that it may affect sex differentiation; limited human case reports have not shown an association with major malformations [3].

Spironolactone and its active metabolites competitively bind aldosterone receptors in the distal nephron, increasing sodium and water excretion while retaining potassium [3]. Its antiandrogen action comes from weak antagonism of androgen receptors and reduced androgen production, which is the rationale for sebum and acne effects [1][2]. Wikipedia notes it is only a weak diuretic on its own [1].

Spironolactone was discovered in 1957 and introduced in 1959; Grokipedia attributes its development to G.D. Searle and a first US approval in 1960 [1][2]. RALES in 1999 established its role in severe heart failure [7]. It is on the WHO Essential Medicines List and was the 52nd most prescribed drug in the US in 2023, according to Wikipedia [1].

lore.intro: Spironolactone is discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a topical anti-androgen for acne and skin texture during anabolic steroid use, and on T Nation in lists of drugs that affect hormones or breast tissue [19][21].

claims.claim: Topical spironolactone prevents steroid-related acne and poor skin texture without affecting hormone levels.
claims.believers: The author of a looksmax.org thread says a 2% to 5% prescription-grade cream or gel counters androgenic skin effects during a steroid cycle and, applied to the skin, does not lower testosterone [19]. A T Nation poster likewise says he had heard spironolactone cream is an effective topical anti-androgen for back acne [22].
claims.experts: A 2023 systematic review examined oral and topical spironolactone for androgen-related skin conditions [11]. The sources reviewed contain no trials in people using anabolic steroids.

claims.claim: Oral spironolactone helps hair loss caused by DHT.
claims.believers: The same looksmax.org thread says oral spironolactone can be tried for DHT-related hair loss while stating that finasteride or dutasteride is generally a better option [19].
claims.experts: A systematic review of androgenetic alopecia treatments and a review of oral and topical spironolactone describe the evidence as coming mainly from small studies [11][12].

claims.claim: Spironolactone can reduce water retention caused by growth hormone use.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster in a thread on growth hormone, quoted in the excerpt, says Aldactone helps reduce the high aldosterone and water retention that accompany HGH [20].
claims.experts: The US label describes spironolactone as an aldosterone blocker used as a diuretic in heart failure, cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome, and Wikipedia calls it only a weak diuretic on its own [3][1]. The sources reviewed contain no studies in people using growth hormone.

claims.claim: Spironolactone can cause gynecomastia and lower androgen activity.
claims.believers: A T Nation 'Gyno Sticky' thread lists spironolactone among medications that cause 10 to 20 percent of gynecomastia cases in adults, and a quoted Wikipedia passage in another thread says it reduces testosterone production and blocks androgen receptors [21][20].
claims.experts: The US label lists gynecomastia, hyperkalemia and reduced libido among adverse effects and advises potassium monitoring [3]. Wikipedia describes weak antagonism of the androgen receptor and reduced androgen production [1].
